notes.b: Living things are built from and run by a small set of chemical families. Knowing which family a molecule belongs to, and what food provides, is the starting point for all of cell chemistry.
points: A biomolecule is a molecule made by living organisms. The four main groups are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

All four are organic, which means they are built around chains or rings of carbon atoms bonded to hydrogen. Water and minerals are also chemicals of life but are inorganic, so they do not count as biomolecules. There is more on this in Water and Minerals.
The particular elements found in each biomolecule are listed in Structures of biomolecules.

Food supplies three things: energy, released in respiration (the chemical reactions in cells that release energy from food) mainly from carbohydrates and lipids; raw materials for growth and repair, mainly proteins; and substances that regulate body processes, namely vitamins and minerals.
The body does not take in enzymes and hormones ready made. It makes its own enzymes and hormones from the food it takes in.
notes.tip: Say that biomolecules are organic (carbon and hydrogen based), and that water and minerals are inorganic. Keep structures out of your answer here: that is a different topic.

notes.h: Building and breaking: monomers, polymers and condensation
notes.b: Cells build big molecules by joining small ones together, and break big molecules down again by splitting them. The words monomer, polymer, condensation and hydrolysis name these units and these two opposite reactions.
points: A monomer is a small unit molecule. A polymer is a large molecule made of many monomers joined in a chain.
Monosaccharides (single sugar units) are the monomers of polysaccharides. Amino acids are the monomers of polypeptides and proteins. Nucleotides are the monomers of nucleic acids.
A triglyceride (a fat or oil) is built from glycerol and three fatty acids, but it is not a repeating polymer, because it is not a long chain of identical repeating units.
Condensation: two molecules join and a molecule of water is removed. Glucose units join in this way to form starch, glycogen and cellulose, and amino acids join to form proteins.

Hydrolysis is the reverse: a large molecule is split into smaller ones by adding water, for example starch is hydrolysed to maltose and proteins are hydrolysed to amino acids. Condensation removes water; hydrolysis adds it.

Digestion is hydrolysis catalysed by enzymes (proteins that speed up reactions), which is how food molecules are split into units small enough to absorb. There is more on this in The Digestive System.

Cells assemble biomolecules into the structures they are made of. Cellulose fibres form plant cell walls; phospholipids and proteins form every cell membrane; keratin forms hair and nails; collagen forms skin, tendons and the framework of bone.
Diagram: a chain of linked glucose units. Draw an arrow labelled condensation (water out) joining two units, and an arrow labelled hydrolysis (water in) splitting them. Label monomer and polymer.
notes.tip: Exams can ask you to explain condensation and hydrolysis, and they are useful in structure questions. Remember the simple rule: condensation removes water, hydrolysis adds water.

notes.b: Inside every cell thousands of reactions are going on at once. Together they are called metabolism, and they fall into two opposite kinds: reactions that build up and reactions that break down.
points: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in an organism. Each reaction is controlled by a specific enzyme. Metabolism is one of the characteristics of life.
Anabolism: reactions that build larger, more complex molecules from smaller ones. They need (absorb) energy, because forming bigger molecules is an uphill process.

Anabolic examples: photosynthesis, in which glucose is made from carbon dioxide and water; joining glucose into starch in plants or glycogen in the liver and muscles; and joining amino acids into proteins.
Catabolism: reactions that break larger molecules into smaller ones. They release energy.
Catabolic examples: respiration, in which glucose is broken down to carbon dioxide and water; digestion of starch to maltose and glucose; and breakdown of glycogen to glucose.

Energy transfer: energy released by catabolic reactions such as respiration is used to drive anabolic reactions. It is carried between them by the transfer molecule ATP, a small molecule that delivers energy where the cell needs it.
Catabolism and anabolism therefore depend on each other: catabolism supplies the energy that anabolism needs. There is more on this in Transfer Molecules.
notes.tip: Students often say catabolism uses energy. It is the other way round: catabolism releases energy and anabolism uses it. Do not confuse anabolic reactions with anabolic steroids, which belong to a different topic. When asked why photosynthesis is anabolic, say it builds large molecules from small ones and needs energy; respiration is catabolic.

notes.b: Cells do not only build and break down. They also convert one biomolecule into another, so that a single food or product can supply whatever the cell is short of.
points: Cells convert one biomolecule into another to meet their needs.
Plants make starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, sucrose for transport and oils (for example stored in seeds) from the glucose made in photosynthesis.
Plants absorb nitrogen from the soil as nitrate. Glucose contains no nitrogen, so they use the nitrate, together with glucose, to make amino acids and proteins.
In humans the liver converts excess glucose to glycogen, a storage carbohydrate, and excess carbohydrate is converted to fat for storage.
notes.tip: Be ready to name what a plant turns its glucose into and the job of each product: starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, sucrose for transport, oils in seeds.

notes.b: The two types of metabolism are mirror images of each other. Setting them side by side makes the differences easy to remember.
points: Direction: anabolism joins small molecules into large ones; catabolism breaks large molecules into small ones.
Energy: anabolism needs an input of energy; catabolism releases energy, which is why the two are linked.
Examples: photosynthesis and protein synthesis are anabolic; respiration and digestion are catabolic.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define metabolism, anabolism and catabolism and to give an example of each. Give the direction, the energy change and one named example.

keyTerms.definition: A molecule made by living organisms; the main groups are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
A small unit molecule that is joined to many others to form a polymer.
A large molecule made of many monomers joined in a chain.
A reaction in which two molecules join and a molecule of water is removed.
A reaction in which a large molecule is split into smaller ones by adding water.
The sum of all the chemical reactions in an organism.
Metabolic reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones and need energy.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between anabolism and catabolism, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Anabolism builds larger, more complex molecules from smaller ones and needs energy. An example is photosynthesis, in which glucose is made from carbon dioxide and water. Catabolism breaks larger molecules into smaller ones and releases energy. An example is respiration, in which glucose is broken down to carbon dioxide and water.

questions.prompt: Explain why photosynthesis is described as an anabolic reaction and respiration as a catabolic reaction, and explain how the two kinds of reaction are linked.
questions.model: Photosynthesis is anabolic because it builds the large glucose molecule from small molecules, carbon dioxide and water, and it needs energy. Respiration is catabolic because it breaks glucose down into carbon dioxide and water and releases energy. The two are linked by energy transfer: the energy released by catabolic respiration is carried by ATP and used to drive anabolic reactions, so catabolism and anabolism depend on each other.

questions.prompt: Give two examples of how living cells rearrange biomolecules into new molecules.
questions.model: Plants convert the glucose made in photosynthesis into cellulose, which forms cell walls, and into starch, which is stored. In humans, the liver converts excess glucose into glycogen for storage.
